passage:
Thursday
Back pain woke me before dawn again. I lay there counting what it has taken: the Munnar trek, Sunday cricket, the Bengaluru job I was meant to start this year. Some days it feels like mourning someone who's still alive, and that someone is me. Tonight I snapped at Harsha when she only asked if I wanted tea. I saw her face fall. Later I told her the truth: "It's not you. It's a bad day, and I'm sad about everything I thought I'd be doing." She held my hand and didn't try to fix it.
Things that help, so I remember: the physio's exercises, done slowly; resting before I crash, not after; the follow-up with Dr Mathew next week; saying it out loud instead of snapping.
Jomon

qa.q: What did Harsha ask before Jomon snapped?
qa.a: If Jomon wanted tea.

qa.q: What does Jomon feel about the plans the pain has taken?
qa.a: Jomon feels grief and sadness, like mourning a life that was planned.

qa.q: Which of Jomon's habits support both body and mood?
qa.a: Doing the physio's exercises slowly, resting before crashing, keeping the doctor's follow-up and being honest with Harsha instead of snapping.

qa.q: How was Harsha affected by the snap, and by the honest talk later?
qa.a: Her face fell at the snap over tea, but hearing the truth let her hold Jomon's hand instead of feeling pushed away.

grounding: Shows a young adult with long-lasting pain feeling irritable and grieving lost plans, and pacing, honesty and proper medical care supporting mood.

passage:
Deepika: still on for lunch sunday?
Vaibhav: cancel. sorry
Deepika: pain bad?
Vaibhav: it's always bad. i'm 25 and i walk like dadaji. what's the point of making plans
Deepika: that sounds really heavy. i'm not going anywhere
Vaibhav: i yelled at my flatmate for playing music. he didn't deserve it
Vaibhav: i'm just so tired of being tired
Deepika: that makes sense. you've been carrying this a long time
Deepika: when's your next pain clinic appointment?
Vaibhav: tuesday. i almost cancelled that too
Deepika: don't. i'll come with you if you want
Deepika: and lunch can be at your place. short one. i'll bring khichdi, you stay on the sofa
Vaibhav: ok. thanks didi
Vaibhav: i'll say sorry to my flatmate tonight

qa.q: Who did Vaibhav yell at for playing music?
qa.a: The flatmate.

qa.q: How is Vaibhav feeling about the future?
qa.a: Vaibhav feels hopeless and worn out, "tired of being tired" and doubting the point of making plans.

qa.q: What does Deepika do that supports Vaibhav with dignity?
qa.a: She listens without lecturing, urges keeping the pain clinic appointment and offers to come, and shrinks lunch to a short visit at Vaibhav's place.

qa.q: How might the flatmate have felt about being yelled at?
qa.a: The flatmate was probably hurt or confused, since playing music was ordinary, so Vaibhav's planned apology matters.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult worn down by long-lasting pain feeling hopeless and irritable, with honesty, pacing and medical care keeping life going.

passage: Two years after the bike accident, Naveen's neck still burned by evening, and some mornings he couldn't turn his head to check the traffic. He had planned to be a wedding photographer, hauling cameras across Hyderabad every weekend. Now even an hour behind a lens left him flat on the bed. On Saturday Vandana asked if he wanted to go to her cousin's engagement, and he snapped, "Do I look like I can go anywhere?" Then he lay staring at the fan, ashamed. That night he told her the truth: "I'm not angry with you. I'm grieving the job I thought I'd have." Vandana sat beside him. "Then let's plan around the pain, not against it." On Monday they went back to his pain specialist together and agreed on regular physiotherapy. He took on one small portrait shoot a month, with rest breaks written into the schedule.

qa.q: What had Naveen planned to be?
qa.a: A wedding photographer.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as he lay staring at the fan?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of snapping and full of grief for the photography career he had planned.

qa.q: What steps support Naveen's mood as well as his neck?
qa.a: Being honest with Vandana, returning to his pain specialist for physiotherapy, and pacing his work with one shoot a month and rest breaks.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt when Naveen snapped about the engagement?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt at first, but she listened and offered to plan around the pain with him.

grounding: Shows a young adult with long-lasting pain feeling irritable and grieving a planned life, and finding dignity through honesty, pacing and medical care.

passage:
"Uma, you left the dishes again."
"I know, Samir. I'll do them tomorrow."
"You said that yesterday."
"And yesterday my hips hurt so much I sat on the bathroom floor for twenty minutes. Do you want the details?"
"No. Sorry. I didn't know it was that bad."
"It's always that bad. I just don't announce it."
"You used to run every morning."
"Don't. I know. I had a half-marathon planned for this year. Now I'm grieving my own legs."
"That sounds awful."
"It is. And then I snap at you over dishes and hate myself for it."
"Okay. What if we split things differently? I do dishes, you do the grocery orders and the stuff you can do sitting down."
"You'd do that?"
"Obviously. And you go to that follow-up with the specialist next week. I'll drive."
"Deal. And Samir? Thanks for asking instead of just being annoyed."

qa.q: Where did Uma sit for twenty minutes yesterday?
qa.a: On the bathroom floor.

qa.q: What does Uma mean by "grieving my own legs"?
qa.a: Uma feels deep grief and frustration at losing the running life, including a planned half-marathon, to long-lasting pain.

qa.q: How does the new split of chores help?
qa.a: It paces Uma's activity to what the pain allows while keeping Uma contributing, alongside the specialist follow-up.

qa.q: How does Samir's view change during the talk?
qa.a: Samir moves from annoyance about the dishes to understanding how bad the pain is, and offers practical help.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose long-lasting pain brings grief and irritability, and honesty, pacing and medical follow-up supporting mood and dignity.

passage: The first year of living with pain, I was mostly angry. I'm Nikita, and I was twenty-three when the ache in my lower back stopped going away after a fall on the hospital stairs. I'd planned night shifts, travel nursing, maybe Canada. Instead I was counting how many minutes I could stand. I snapped at Dhruv when he offered to carry my bag, cried when a friend posted beach photos, and slept badly, which made everything worse. What changed wasn't a miracle. My physiotherapist taught me pacing: work, rest, stretch, before the pain peaked, not after. I told Dhruv the truth, that his help sometimes made me feel useless, and we agreed he'd ask first. I switched to a day-clinic job. Some days are still grey. But I've stopped measuring my life against the one I planned, and I'm less furious at everyone, including myself.

qa.q: What did the physiotherapist teach Nikita?
qa.a: Pacing: work, rest, stretch, before the pain peaked, not after.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel during the first year?
qa.a: Nikita felt mostly angry, grieving the planned life of night shifts and travel nursing.

qa.q: Which changes supported Nikita's mood?
qa.a: Pacing from the physiotherapist, being honest with Dhruv about the help, and moving to a day-clinic job.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt when Nikita snapped about the bag?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt hurt and confused, since he was only trying to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult with long-lasting pain feeling angry and grieving a planned life, and pacing, honesty and proper care supporting mood.

passage:
Counsellor's session note, Shreya, week 4
Shreya arrived late and irritable, snapping that 'these sessions won't fix my joints anyway.' Then she cried. She has lived with joint pain for two years and talks about the dance career she had planned as if it has died. She is exhausted, angry at her body and feels guilty for snapping at her mother. We talked about pacing: breaking her day into short blocks with rest, instead of pushing hard on good days and crashing after. She agreed to tell her mother honestly how the pain feels, and to keep her appointment with her specialist next week. She left calmer. We will continue weekly.
Payal

qa.q: What did Shreya say about the sessions?
qa.a: That 'these sessions won't fix my joints anyway.'

qa.q: What is Shreya grieving, and how does she feel about it?
qa.a: She is grieving the dance career she had planned, and feels exhausted, angry at her body and guilty for snapping at her mother.

qa.q: What plan did Shreya and Payal agree on?
qa.a: Pacing her day in short blocks with rest, telling her mother honestly about the pain, and keeping the specialist appointment.

qa.q: How might Shreya's mother experience the snapping?
qa.a: Her mother may feel hurt or helpless, not knowing how much the pain drains Shreya until they talk honestly.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young woman whose long-lasting pain brings exhaustion, anger and grief, and supports pacing, honesty and medical care.
